terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to try the shop's price rules on a few prices.

tasks.title: Write it the short way
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/callbacks.js`, rewrite `addWrapping` as an arrow function kept in a `const` with the same name. It still takes `cents` and returns `cents` plus 350.

Check calls `addWrapping` with other prices and makes sure it is kept in a `const` and written with `=>`.
nextSteps: Read the lesson's part on arrow functions.
Write `const addWrapping =`, then the parameter, `=>` and the sum.
Delete the old `function addWrapping` so the name is made only once.
Run the file: the first line should not change.
hints: An arrow function is a shorter way to write a function. You keep it in a variable, like any value.
Without curly braces after `=>`, the value after it is given back by itself, no `return` needed. A name can be made only once, so the old function has to go.
The line has the shape `const addWrapping = (cents) => ...`, with the sum in place of the dots.

tasks.title: Pick the rule for the day
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `ruleFor(day)` return `weekendRule` when `day` is `'Saturday'` or `'Sunday'`, and `weekdayRule` for any other day. It returns the rule itself, a function, not a price.

Check calls `ruleFor` with both weekend days and two weekdays, and looks at which function comes back.
nextSteps: Look at the two rules above `ruleFor`: they are functions kept in `const`s.
Ask whether `day` is one of the two weekend days.
Return the right rule by its name, with no round brackets after it.
Run the file: the line for Task 2 should name a function.
hints: A function is a value. You can return it like a number or a text.
With round brackets after its name, a function runs and you get its answer. Without them you have the function itself, which is what `ruleFor` hands back.
The function has the shape `if (day === 'Saturday' || day === 'Sunday') { return weekendRule }`, then `return weekdayRule`.

tasks.title: Apply any rule
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `applyRule(priceCents, rule)` call `rule` with `priceCents` and return what `rule` gives back.

Check calls `applyRule` with prices and rules of its own, written as arrow functions.
nextSteps: Remember that `rule` is a function, handed in like any other value.
Call it with `priceCents` between its round brackets.
Run the file and try `weekdayRule` in place of `weekendRule`.
hints: A parameter can hold a function. Inside, you call it by the parameter's name.
`rule` without brackets is the function; `rule(priceCents)` runs it on the price and gives its answer.
The body is one line: `return rule(priceCents)`.

tasks.title: Count what passes a test
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, make `countWhere(text, test)` go through every character of `text`, call `test` with it, and return how many characters `test` gave back `true` for.

Check calls `countWhere` with texts and tests of its own, an empty text and a test that is never true included.
nextSteps: Go through `text` with `for...of`, as in the issue on loops.
For each character, call `test` with it and count one when it gives back true.
Return the count and run the file.
hints: This is the counting loop you know, with one change: the question about each character comes from `test`.
`test` alone is a function and always counts as true. Call it with the character to get its answer.
Inside the loop, `if (test(character)) { count++ }`, with `count` made before the loop.
